purpose: Tiopronin is used to prevent kidney stones made of a substance called cystine in people who have a condition called cystinuria. It is usually tried when drinking lots of water and following a special diet have not been enough to stop stones from forming. It helps protect your kidneys and urinary tract from damage caused by these stones.
how_it_works: People with cystinuria have too much of an amino acid called cystine in their urine, which clumps together and forms hard stones. Tiopronin works by chemically bonding to cystine in your urine, turning it into a more soluble form that dissolves easily and can be flushed out when you urinate. Think of it like a helper that grabs onto the stone-forming substance and makes it harmless so it can leave your body safely.
common_side_effects: Nausea, vomiting, stomach upset, diarrhea, or loss of appetite are fairly common. Some people notice skin rashes, itching, or a change in the taste of food. You may also see a mild fever, joint pain, or mouth sores, especially early in treatment.
warnings: Tiopronin can rarely cause serious problems including kidney disease (proteinuria), low blood cell counts, and liver issues, so your doctor will do regular blood and urine tests while you are on this medicine. Tell your doctor right away if you notice swelling, unusual bruising or bleeding, yellowing of the skin or eyes, or difficulty breathing. Pregnant women should avoid this medication as it may harm the baby. Always drink plenty of fluids — at least 8 glasses of water a day — while taking this medicine.
typical_dosing: Adults usually start at 800 mg per day, taken in divided doses (for example, about 267 mg three times a day). The dose is then adjusted based on how much cystine is in your urine, and some people may need up to 1,000 mg or more per day. Children's doses are based on body weight. Take it on an empty stomach, at least 30 minutes before or 2 hours after a meal, unless your doctor tells you otherwise.
